studies.title: Model scene: The electric meter runs out
studies.plain: Practice for the style "Kitchen-sink realism": on a rainy weeknight in a small rented flat, a warehouse worker who has just been suspended over a missed shift tells her teenage son, while the prepaid electric meter runs out. They argue across the kitchen table in the dark, and a small kindness ends it.

beats.note: she comes in still wearing the warehouse tabard; he is doing homework at the table, a pan of beans on the hob
she unpins her name badge and drops it in the fruit bowl, then stirs his beans, asking about his maths

studies.title: Model scene: The last crossing of the ferry cafe
studies.plain: Practice for the style "Deadpan stillness and long pauses": on a small night ferry, the cook in the onboard cafe and the one lorry driver who eats there every night sit through the cafe's very last crossing before it closes for good. Nobody moves, nobody shows a thing, an old song plays on the jukebox, a crash in the kitchen gets no reaction at all, and a sad fact said flatly is the funniest line in the scene.

beats.note: an empty ferry cafe at night: the cook behind the counter, one lorry driver at a table by the window, the engines humming
'I'll have whatever is going.' A long wait while she wipes the counter. 'Everything is going. We close tomorrow.'
he puts a coin in the jukebox and taps one finger on the table; a beat later, behind the counter, she taps the same rhythm on the till
the boat rolls and, in the kitchen we never see, every cup slides off a shelf one after another; neither of them moves. 'That was the cups.'
out on deck under one bulb, their breath in the cold; he asks what she will do now, and after a long time she shrugs
the ferry docks. 'Same time tomorrow, then.' 'No.' A long pause. They both nod, and he walks down to his lorry

studies.title: Model scene: A tuba at the lost property office
studies.plain: Practice for the style "Deadpan stillness and long pauses": on a rainy afternoon, a shy man comes to a small railway lost property office to claim the tuba he left on the 9:40 train. The clerk behind the hatch never moves her face, answers every question with total seriousness and never once gets the joke, while a lost dog in a basket watches them both and steals the one musical moment.

beats.note: shelves of umbrellas, one lone dog in a basket, a man at the hatch; the clerk does not look up
'I left a tuba on the 9:40.' A very long pause. 'Which tuba?'
she rings the depot; we hear only a faint voice; she says 'yes' six times, hangs up, and says 'They have no tuba.'

studies.title: Model scene: The sealed case on the night train
studies.plain: Practice for steering attention in a thriller: a courier must carry a sealed case from one end of a night train to the other before the border stop, and she has been told one rule: never let it touch the floor. studies.title: Model scene: The best man's shuffled speech cards
studies.plain: Practice for steering attention in a comedy: a nervous best man drops his speech cards on the way to the microphone and reads them in the wrong order. first card: '...and that's why she said no the first time.' Second card: 'Thank you all for coming to the funeral.' He keeps going.

studies.title: Model scene: Two people close the bookshop for the last time
studies.plain: Practice for steering attention in a romance: two coworkers who have circled each other for years work the last shift before their small bookshop closes for good. A slow middle stretch where they just pack boxes is kept on purpose as a rest, every question one of them answers opens a bigger one, and the kiss the whole film has been holding back finally comes, then gets turned on its head.

beats.note: the shop at dusk, half its shelves empty; an old record on the counter player; they tape boxes and do not look at each other
a quiet stretch: books into boxes, the tape gun, the record crackling; nothing happens and we are let to rest in it
'Are you taking the job in the city?' 'Yes.' 'Why?' 'Because there was no reason to stay.' 'Was there ever?'
she finds a book behind the till with a bus ticket in it, marked at the page they argued about on her first day
they kiss at last, and it is she who pulls back first: 'I'm still going.'
he holds out the shop key; she takes it, locks the door with both of them on the outside, and keeps it

studies.title: Model scene: The treehouse map with one rule
studies.plain: Practice for steering attention in a kids' adventure: three friends find a map in their new treehouse, signed by a kid who lived there long ago, with one rule written across the top: never follow it after the streetlights come on. The opening promises a treasure hunt, each clue they solve opens a bigger question, and the rule they learned at the start is broken on purpose at the end.

beats.note: the camera rises up a huge oak to a crooked treehouse; a gust lifts a floorboard and a rolled up map falls at their feet
the map, held up to the light long enough for us to read the rule along the top: NEVER FOLLOW AFTER THE STREETLIGHTS COME ON
the first X is a garden gnome; under it, a key; the key opens the old shed; in the shed, a second map, drawn in the same hand but dated last week
they reach the last X at the end of the lane as the sky goes orange; in the corner of each shot, the streetlight at the end of the road
the streetlight flickers on. They look at each other. The youngest says 'We're so close' and takes the first step
every streetlight down the lane comes on at once, and the hedges part to show a path that was not there in the day

studies.title: Model scene: The beekeeper on the morning of the first frost
studies.plain: Practice for steering attention in a quiet documentary-style scene: an old beekeeper checks her hives on the first frosty morning of the year, talking now and then to the camera. The opening tells us plainly this will be slow and calm, long still shots give us time to read every corner, the eye is passed gently from hive to hive across the cuts, and the few small surprises are spaced far apart.

beats.note: frost on a field at dawn; her voice over: 'This might be my last winter with them. I want to see how they do.'
three hives in a row, each shot held still; she looks off toward the next hive, and the next shot has it in the center where our eye already rests
she lifts lids, puts an ear to the wood, writes in a notebook; minutes pass with no question pulling us on
the small surprise that ends the lull: one bee walks out onto the frosty landing board and sits in the sun

values.surpriseSpacing.fair: fully set up, we could have guessed

beats.note: she laughs at the bee, and says to the camera 'Tougher than me, that one,' and her voice catches

values.surpriseSpacing.fair: fully set up, we could have guessed

beats.note: she walks back across the white field toward the house; the camera stays with the hives as the frost begins to melt

values.surpriseSpacing.fair: fully set up, we could have guessed

studies.title: Model scene: The vending machine in the hospital corridor
studies.plain: Late at night, a grown son waits in a hospital corridor while his father is in surgery. He braces for the news, the vending machine eats his coins, and when the doctor comes he goes completely numb and asks something calm and silly. His sister arrives in tears and he cannot meet her. Only when the machine finally drops the chocolate bar he paid for an hour ago does the feeling break through.

beats.note: a long empty corridor at two in the morning; one man on a plastic chair keeps doing up and undoing the top button of his coat
he feeds the vending machine a coin for a chocolate bar; the coil turns and the bar hangs on the edge, not falling. He says 'Of course' to nobody
the doctor speaks just out of frame and her words go dull and far away; we only see his face. Then, quite calmly: 'Does that machine give change?'
his sister runs in crying and throws her arms round him; he stands with his arms at his sides and tells her the parking is free after midnight
with a clunk the chocolate bar finally drops; he laughs once, too loud, and then he is crying into his sister's shoulder
the two of them on the plastic chairs, splitting the chocolate bar in silence, small at the end of the long corridor

studies.title: Model scene: Dad irons everything on the wedding morning
studies.plain: On the morning of his daughter's wedding, the house is in a panic and the bride is the only calm one. Her father cannot sit still, so he irons: his shirt, then the tea towels, then the dog's blanket, while muttering his speech to the ironing board. When he scorches the veil, the bride and her father trade places: she panics, and he goes perfectly calm and fixes it.

beats.note: a small house full of aunts, flowers and hairspray; everyone shouts about the cars, and the bride eats toast in her dressing gown. In the corner, her dad irons his shirt
he has moved on to the tea towels, all of them, folded into sharp squares. The bride, chewing: 'Dad, they're tea towels.' 'They're going to be smart tea towels'
now ironing the dog's blanket, he mutters his speech to the board: 'When she was small...' and the line fades every time at the same spot; the aunt holding the dog's lead hears it
a burning smell; the music cuts out. He lifts the iron off the veil. For the first time all morning, the bride screams. He puts the iron down very gently: 'Right. My turn to be calm, then'
he snips out the scorch mark and folds the hole into a neat little heart, steady hands for once; the whole house goes quiet and watches
they head for the car, the bride in her mended veil; behind them the dog trots past wearing a neatly ironed tea towel

values.sceneButton: the biggest laugh of the scene

studies.title: Model scene: The last box on moving day
studies.plain: A mother and her teenage son move out of the family house, sold because of money trouble neither of them mentions. She chats brightly with the removal men all day, and he finds a tape his absent father once made and hides it in his coat. The feeling only hits her hours later, in the car, when he plays the tape and a song from a happier time comes on.

beats.note: half-empty rooms that echo; the mother makes tea for the removal men and talks about the weather far too much
in the dark loft, by torchlight, the son finds a tape labelled in his dad's writing, 'For the car'. He slips it into his coat
a removal man, carrying the sofa: 'Big house to give up, this.' She asks him at once if he takes sugar. He says he has already had four teas
the last box goes out; she stands in the empty kitchen, turns away from the door when he calls her, and then turns back smiling: 'Ready'
at a red light he pushes the tape in and a cheerful old pop song fills the car; she cries quietly at the wheel. He says, not looking at her: 'It's not your fault. The money'
the light turns green; she laughs, wipes her face and turns the song up, and the camera rises as the car pulls away up the hill

studies.title: Model scene: The tree in the school play
studies.plain: A shy boy has been cast as a tree in the school play. His gruff father, who claims he only came for the free biscuits, secretly stayed up all night building a huge tree costume. On stage the costume knocks over the scenery, the boy's fear and his father's calm swap places, and we watch the whole disaster on the father's face.

beats.note: a school hall on folding chairs, a teacher thumping the piano; in the front row a big man in a work jacket eats a biscuit and looks bored
the mum beside him notices glue and green paint all over his knuckles. 'Late night?' 'Biscuits are free,' he says, not looking at her
the tree waddles on, far too big; one branch takes out the cardboard castle, the next takes out the moon, and the whole set comes down slowly, piece by piece
we stay on the father's face as we hear the hall fall silent; a small voice from the stage: 'Um. A storm came.' His face goes from horror to hope
the boy, no longer afraid, plays the storm too: he sways and howls and the hall roars; his father, who now cannot sit still, wipes his eyes on his sleeve
the mum next to him offers a tissue. 'Hay fever,' he says. 'In December,' she says, and he takes the tissue

studies.title: Model scene: Two brothers and no fish
studies.plain: Two brothers who have not spoken properly in years go fishing at dawn on a still lake. They catch nothing. The younger one shouts at a tangled reel because he cannot shout at his brother, who is ill and has not said so. Their trust grows one small joke at a time, and the big news, when it finally comes, is just a whisper and a nod.

beats.note: two men in a small rowing boat in the mist, back to back with their rods, saying nothing at all
a duck swims up and eats the bait straight off the hook. A long pause. 'That's the most action we've had.' 'He's doing better than us.' The first shared smile
the younger one sees the pill box in his brother's bag and says nothing; a minute later his reel tangles and he shouts at it, long and loud, until a heron flies off
the older one quietly untangles the reel for him, slowly, knot by knot. The younger one says sorry; his brother shrugs
a long silence over the water. Then, very quietly, looking at his float: 'It's back.' His brother nods once, small, and keeps watching his own float
the sun comes up over the lake; they sit shoulder to shoulder now. The duck comes back and sits on the end of the boat as if it were one of them

studies.title: Model scene: The seventh birthday and the empty chair
studies.plain: A girl turns seven at a crowded, noisy party. Her grandad, who never missed a birthday, died in the spring, and her grandmother still sets his plate at the table. She smiles for the room in his old cardigan while everyone else is laughing. Only the birthday girl notices, and she brings her grandmother the first slice of cake.

beats.note: balloons, a paper tablecloth, kids everywhere; at the head of the long table one chair stays empty, a party hat and a plate set in front of it
the hired magician pulls the wrong card three times and the kids shriek with joy; at the edge of the frame the grandmother, in a man's baggy cardigan, laughs a beat too late
from the girl's height: her grandmother pours tea into the cup at the empty place, then stops, the pot still in the air; the party noise fades to one clock ticking
the girl carries over the first slice of cake, not to her own place but to her grandmother. 'He'd want the first bit. You eat it for him'

values.caretaker.whom: someone who does not deserve it

beats.note: she eats the cake with her eyes shining; then she starts the birthday song herself, loud and off-key, and the whole room joins in

values.caretaker.whom: someone who does not deserve it
values.moodOutOfStep.ends: they give in to the room

beats.note: later, the room cleared: the cardigan now hangs on the back of the empty chair, and the girl's balloon is tied to it

studies.title: Model scene: The night bus home after the party
studies.plain: A young woman leaves her own leaving party, the best night she has had in years, and rides the night bus home alone with the glow wearing off by the stop. A rowdy hen party sings at the back while she sits in silence. Her card fails, and the driver quietly takes the blame when an inspector gets on. She never thanks him, and only works it out as the bus pulls away.

beats.note: a pub doorway, hugs and shouting, the music still pounding inside; she waves goodbye to everyone, the door shuts and the music stops dead
alone under one street lamp at the bus stop, still in her party hat; the night bus hisses up
her card beeps red; the driver waves her on without looking up. At the back, a hen party in matching sashes sings a love song badly, and the bride-to-be is wearing a traffic cone
she leans her head on the cold window and watches her own face in the glass; behind her, the hen party's song goes on, far too happy. One of them, in a veil, glances at her
an inspector gets on and asks to see her pass; the driver calls back that his machine has been broken all night, his fault, and takes the telling-off. The bride-to-be offers her a sausage roll
at her stop, she sees the card machine light up green as the next passenger taps on. She turns, but the bus is already pulling away, the hen party waving from the back window

studies.title: Model scene: The last day of the hardware shop
studies.plain: An old man closes his hardware shop for good after forty years, with the teenage assistant he spent the whole film pretending not to like. He keeps busy, fixing a drawer that will never be opened again. He snaps at a customer haggling over one screw, when the anger is really for the big store across the road. At the end, he hands the girl his old tape measure with nothing but a nod.

beats.note: a narrow shop with a thousand little drawers; a CLOSING DOWN sign in the window. The old man is mending a drawer that sticks
the girl: 'We close in an hour. Nobody will ever open that drawer again.' He keeps screwing: 'Then it'll be shut properly'

a man asks for a discount on one screw, 'since you're closing'; the old man slams the drawer so hard every drawer on the wall rattles. Then, quietly: 'Sorry. It's free. Everything's free. Take a hammer'
through the window, across the road, the giant new store glows; his screwdriver slips. The girl puts her hand over his and takes the screwdriver away
he takes the battered brass tape measure off his belt, puts it in her hand and gives one small nod. She nods back. Nobody says a word
they lock up together; she measures the door on the way out. 'Two metres and four.' 'Two metres and five,' he says. 'It sticks.' The door sticks

studies.title: Model scene: Who jammed the office printer
studies.plain: In an open-plan office the printer jams for the ninth time this week. The boss's loyal right hand decides it must be the new temp, and the whole room quietly goes along with it. Nobody helps her as she climbs half inside the machine. In the end the printer coughs out the real culprit: three hundred copies of the right hand's holiday photo.

beats.note: twelve desks, one printer blinking red. Beside the boss's door stands his right hand, holding a coffee like a badge
'Did you print something big?' he asks the temp. 'Did you see me print something big?' 'Did you see me see you?' Everyone else looks relieved it is not them
she climbs half inside the printer, legs sticking out; a slow pan along eleven colleagues all suddenly fascinated by their screens

values.quietMajority.shot: a slow pan along all of them

beats.note: from inside the machine, to the paper tray: 'It's fine. I'm sure everyone here would have helped if their phones weren't so interesting.' Eleven people go stiff at once

values.quietMajority.shot: a slow pan along all of them

beats.note: the jam clears and the printer spits out page after page: the right hand in swimming trunks on a beach, three hundred times. He gathers them up without a word

values.quietMajority.shot: a slow pan along all of them
values.sceneButton: the biggest laugh of the scene

studies.title: Model scene: The new drummer's first rehearsal
studies.plain: Three old friends in a garage band try out a new drummer. The singer and the guitarist finish each other's sentences, they all share a joke nobody will explain, and the drummer talks like a museum guide. To be let in, he must eat the bassist's legendary week-old chili. He does, and when he finally says the joke phrase by accident, the band goes silent and then cheers.

beats.note: a garage full of cables and a sofa with no legs. 'We used to have a drummer who...' 'who only played in socks.' 'Like Tuesday.' They both laugh. The new drummer smiles politely
'Good evening. I shall begin with a modest shuffle in four four, if that suits.' The bassist mouths 'shall' to the singer
the bassist brings out a pot of chili 'from last Sunday.' Three faces watch him lift the spoon. He chews for a long time
they play at last; the guitarist goes wrong and the drummer, sweating chili, yells 'Oh come ON, that's like Tuesday!' The music stops dead
silence, then all three cheer. 'Nobody's ever told him what Tuesday was,' says the singer. 'I shall not be asking,' says the drummer

values.insideJoke.outsider: an outsider is let in on it

studies.title: Model scene: The drive home from the exam
studies.plain: A mother drives her teenage son home from his final exam while his two little sisters fight in the back. He is sure he failed and dodges every question about it. She hears her own mother's warnings in her head and fights not to repeat them. When he finally says it went badly, she admits she failed the same exam once, and the car goes quiet in a good way.

beats.note: mother and son in front, eyes on the road; in the back the sisters go 'Did.' 'Didn't.' 'Did.' 'Didn't' getting quieter each time
'So how was it?' 'Want a crisp?' 'How was the...' 'These are cheese ones.' In his head we see him, aged forty, still sitting the same exam

values.dodgedQuestion.tool: an offer of food or drink

beats.note: her own mother's voice echoes: 'If you don't push him, nobody will.' She opens her mouth, then shuts it. In the back, one sister just goes 'Hmph'

values.dodgedQuestion.tool: an offer of food or drink

beats.note: 'I think I failed.' She keeps driving. 'I failed it the first time too. Your gran didn't speak to me for a week.' He turns to look at her for the first time

values.dodgedQuestion.tool: an offer of food or drink

beats.note: the car rolls on in an easy quiet, until a small voice from the back: 'Did.'

studies.title: Model scene: A brother's letter in the courtroom
studies.plain: At a sentencing hearing, a man who stole from his brother's bakery to keep his own family afloat sits and tells his lawyer he is fine. He has always been the one who holds everyone together. His brother stands and reads a letter he wrote the night before, voice shaking. Only then does the man see what he became, and his apology comes after the bakery is already gone.

beats.note: a quiet courtroom. His lawyer leans in: 'All right?' 'I'm fine.' Under the table his hands twist a paper cup into a rope

values.selfStory.role: the one who holds it together

beats.note: his brother stands with one folded page: 'I am not here to make you suffer. I am here because I miss you.' We watch the man listening, not the brother reading

values.selfStory.role: the one who holds it together

beats.note: the brother reaches the line about their father's oven and has to stop. The whole room waits. The man drops the twisted cup

values.selfStory.role: the one who holds it together

beats.note: asked if he wishes to speak, he stands and says only: 'I told myself I was saving us. I was saving me. The bakery's gone and I can't bring it back'

values.selfStory.role: the one who holds it together

beats.note: the brother folds the letter and, on his way past, sets it on the man's table. Neither looks at the other. The room empties around it

values.selfStory.role: the one who holds it together

studies.title: Model scene: Asking at the summer camp dance
studies.plain: On the last night of summer camp, a shy twelve-year-old has rehearsed asking a girl to dance with his bunkmate holding a canoe paddle as stand-in. He weighs every option until the slow song is nearly over, starts to say he likes her and swerves into her shoes. She asks him first. The camp counselor notices he has changed all summer.

beats.note: behind the boat shed, he bows to a canoe paddle his bunkmate holds upright: 'Would you, perhaps, like to...' 'It's a paddle, man.' 'Again'
the slow song starts in the mess hall. We hear his thoughts: walk over, wait, wave, pretend to need punch, leave camp forever. His bunkmate has already asked three people
a deep breath, and he crosses the floor. 'Hi. I really li... like... your shoes.' She looks down at her muddy camp boots. 'Thanks?'
'So do you want to dance or not?' she says. He nods so hard his cap falls off
his big sister, a counselor, watches from the door: 'Look at that. In June he wouldn't order his own pancakes.' Behind her, the bunkmate slow dances with the paddle

studies.title: Model scene: A brand new me at the hair salon
studies.plain: Just after a breakup, a woman sits in the salon chair and announces she is a completely new person, so it is all off or nothing. The stylist chatters on while she answers in single words, and keeps checking her ex's photos. Over the roar of a hen party and the hairdryers, the stylist whispers to her colleague. In the end she asks for exactly the same cut as always, and feels a little new anyway.

beats.note: she sits down hard. 'New me. Totally new. Either it all comes off or don't touch it.' The stylist holds up two fingers' worth of hair: 'This much?' 'ALL'
the stylist talks for forty seconds about fringes, holidays and her cousin's rabbit. 'Mm.' Meanwhile the client scrolls her ex's photos under the cape, three times
a hen party cheers in the next chairs, hairdryers roar; the stylist leans to her colleague's ear. We catch only: '...every time... same cut... crying in the car...'
now she talks and talks, about him, his mother, his terrible boat, and the stylist just says 'Mm.' Then: 'Could you do the usual? But, like, newer?'
she looks in the mirror at exactly the same haircut and gasps: 'I look like a whole different woman.' The stylist, deadpan: 'Mm'

values.sceneButton: the biggest laugh of the scene

studies.title: Model scene: The cabin door on the night ferry
studies.plain: On a night ferry back to the island where his wife died, an old sailor who swore never to go back locks himself in his cabin. His grown daughter sits on the deck outside and talks to him through the door. He keeps replaying his last goodbye at the harbor. When she says she is staying on the island, he stops wanting to run, calls her by her childhood name, and opens the door.

beats.note: wind across the deck, the engine thudding. She knocks on cabin twelve: 'Dad, you said you'd never go back. Well, we're going back.' Nothing
inside, he sits against the door; the harbor goodbye flashes by three times, and each time he says something kinder before the boat leaves. Outside, she sits against the same door
'I'm not coming back with you, Dad. I've taken Mum's old house. I'm staying.' Only the engine answers for a long time
through the door, very softly, just: 'Pip.' She stops breathing. Nobody has called her that since she was six
the lock clicks. He steps out in his coat, and they stand at the rail together as the island lights come up out of the dark

studies.title: Model scene: The job interview in her second language
studies.plain: A young woman interviews for an office job in her second language. She rehearsed every answer in the bus window and hears her old piano teacher telling her to sit up straight. She says she is not nervous while her foot taps like a drum. When she drops her pen and swears in her first language, the interviewer answers in the same language, and the whole interview turns.

beats.note: her mouthed bus window answers cut against the real ones. In her ear, an old voice: 'Back straight. Hands still.' She sits up like a soldier

values.rehearsedLine.shown: cut together with the real moment

beats.note: 'Do you get nervous under pressure?' 'Never.' Under the desk her foot taps so fast the water glass shivers. He glances down at it

values.rehearsedLine.shown: cut together with the real moment

beats.note: asked where she sees herself in five years, she gives her perfect answer to 'What is your greatest weakness?' word for word. A pause. 'That's... also useful'

values.rehearsedLine.shown: cut together with the real moment

beats.note: her pen rolls away and she swears under her breath in her first language. The interviewer answers in the same language: 'My mother says that one too.' They both stay in it

values.rehearsedLine.shown: cut together with the real moment

beats.note: laughing now, she slumps back in the chair at last; her foot is still. On her way out she shakes hands with the coat stand
